paragraphs: This paper examines whether language models reproduce a statistical structure of human language that extends beyond individual words or sentences. The structure concerns information complexity, measured in bits per token: its patterns resemble themselves at different scales, and dependencies persist over long distances. The authors investigate whether generated text shares these fractal characteristics.

They examine how decoding temperature and prompting affect the results, identifying conditions under which models may fail to reproduce these properties. Human language exhibits fractal parameters within a relatively narrow range, while the parameters of generated text vary much more widely. These findings hold across several model architectures, suggesting that the observed differences are not confined to one particular model.

The authors also release more than 240,000 generated articles with corresponding human texts. Their findings suggest that fractal measurements could help identify a non-trivial portion of generated writing. This is a possible detection signal, alongside a way to study how generation choices influence the statistical structure of synthetic language.
icml-2025-a-tale-of-two-structures-do-ll.tldr: Language-model outputs vary more widely than human text in fractal complexity, suggesting a possible signal for detecting some generated writing.

paragraphs: Multimodal learning seeks representations that connect information across different kinds of input. Contrastive losses are widely used for this purpose, yet the resulting representation spaces can remain poorly aligned. This paper argues that information specific to each modality helps explain the mismatch: representations can share useful information while still retaining substantial modality-dependent content.

The authors analyze this issue through the Information Bottleneck Principle. Some common contrastive objectives maximize mutual information between modalities, but that goal does not itself remove information unique to either one. The distinction matters because encouraging shared content and suppressing modality-specific content are different requirements. The paper also uses controlled experiments to examine how hyperparameters influence the emergence of misalignment.

Building on this analysis, the authors derive an additional regularization term using a variational approximation. Its purpose is to improve alignment of the learned representations. They investigate its advantages in both controlled settings and real-world applications, connecting a theoretical explanation of misalignment to a concrete modification of the training objective.
icml-2025-aligning-multimodal-representa.tldr: The paper explains multimodal misalignment through retained modality-specific information and develops an information-bottleneck regularizer intended to improve alignment.

paragraphs: The value of producing data depends on the decisions it will support and the information its buyer already has. This paper develops a valuation framework incorporating both factors. It connects the framework to economic theories of signals and information design, giving the valuation a foundation in how information helps an agent make decisions.

For Bayesian linear regression, the proposed value becomes information gain. The authors then study how a monopoly seller can price data in that setting. If the seller can completely customize data production, they show that the seller can capture the full available surplus from any population of buyers. This is the strongest revenue outcome considered, corresponding to first-degree price discrimination.

Restricting production to an existing data pool changes the result: full surplus extraction is generally impossible. The authors nevertheless construct a mechanism whose revenue falls short of that ideal by at most log(κ), where κ is the data matrix's condition number. In the special case of multi-armed bandits, their result yields full surplus extraction.
icml-2025-an-instrumental-value-for-data.tldr: A decision-dependent valuation of data shows how production flexibility determines a monopoly seller's ability to extract buyers' full surplus.

paragraphs: A digital twin simulates how a real system responds to possible actions. Keeping that simulation relevant becomes difficult when the available variables, actions, data, or knowledge change. The paper addresses this changing environment, where conventional approaches can require redesign to handle new variables or retraining to incorporate new information.

The authors formulate digital twinning as in-context learning with a language model. Their system, CALM-DT, uses information supplied at inference time to simulate across different state and action spaces. Fine-tuned encoders retrieve samples for the model's context. This makes retrieval and context construction central to how the twin adapts, while the adaptation itself takes place without updating model parameters.

Experiments show competitive simulation performance compared with existing digital-twin approaches and demonstrate adaptation to changes in the modeling environment. The result supports a different way of maintaining a twin: updating the information available during inference can accommodate changes that would otherwise call for changes to the trained model. The method still uses fine-tuned retrieval encoders as part of its design.
icml-2025-continuously-updating-digital-.tldr: CALM-DT uses retrieved examples and language-model context to adapt digital twins to changing environments without parameter updates during adaptation.

paragraphs: Computing the log-determinant of a large positive definite matrix can be expensive both in arithmetic and in storage. This paper tackles the memory problem with a hierarchical algorithm that performs an LDL decomposition block by block. Organizing the calculation this way makes large-scale log-determinant computation possible under memory constraints.

The authors also address cases where accurately constructing the full matrix is itself infeasible, particularly for highly ill-conditioned kernel matrices. Their analysis includes empirical Neural Tangent Kernels of networks trained on large datasets. Assuming neural scaling laws hold for test error, they derive a power-law relationship for ratios of pseudo-determinants and obtain corresponding scaling laws for estimation.

These relationships allow NTK log-determinants to be estimated using only a small fraction of the full dataset. In the reported experiments, this produces roughly a 100,000-fold speedup while improving accuracy over competing approximations. Together, the blockwise calculation and scaling-based estimation enable work with exceptionally large dense matrices, with the latter approach explicitly depending on the stated scaling-law assumption.
icml-2025-determinant-estimation-under-m.tldr: Blockwise decomposition and conditional neural scaling laws enable log-determinant calculations and estimates for matrices that otherwise exceed practical memory or computation limits.

paragraphs: The maximum independent set problem asks for the largest collection of graph nodes with no edges between them. The authors develop a continuous quadratic objective using the connection between independent sets and cliques in the complementary graph. Adding this clique information is intended to improve convergence and exploration during optimization.

Their analysis shows that every maximal independent set corresponds to a local minimum, derives conditions involving the maximum independent set size, and characterizes stationary points. A maximal set cannot accept another node, but need not be the largest possible set. To navigate the non-convex objective, pCQO-MIS optimizes multiple starting points in parallel with momentum-based gradient descent and uses a checking criterion derived from the theory.

Experiments compare the method with exact, heuristic, sampling, and data-centric approaches. Relative to data-centric methods, it achieves larger independent sets with competitive runtime compared with their inference time, without requiring training data or out-of-distribution tuning. The authors also report that its runtime scales with node count rather than edge count.
icml-2025-differentiable-quadratic-optim.tldr: pCQO-MIS combines a clique-informed quadratic objective with parallel gradient optimization to find large independent sets without training data.

paragraphs: Generated videos can contain convincing individual frames while depicting implausible movement or object interactions. This paper develops a motion-focused evaluation method to capture problems that FVD and other popular video metrics do not measure well. Its central choice is to represent motion through point tracks, following positions through a video.

The method learns motion features by auto-encoding those tracks. These features support comparisons ranging from one generated video against one ground-truth video to comparisons between entire datasets. They can also assess the motion of a single video. This gives the representation uses beyond a single aggregate score comparing two collections of clips.

The authors find that point-track features are more sensitive to synthetic temporal distortions than pixel reconstruction or action-recognition features. They also better predict human judgments of temporal consistency and realism for videos from open-source generators than a wide range of alternatives. Because the representation retains where and when motion occurs, it can localize inconsistencies in space and time, helping explain the errors behind an assessment.
icml-2025-direct-motion-models-for-asses.tldr: A point-track-based video metric better captures motion errors and human judgments while locating inconsistencies in space and time.

paragraphs: Reasoning about objects involves both their individual properties and the relationships between them. This paper separates these into sensory information and relational information. The authors argue that ordinary Transformer attention effectively controls the flow of sensory information, but lacks an explicit mechanism dedicated to routing and processing relationships.

They introduce the Dual Attention Transformer, or DAT, with two distinct attention mechanisms. Sensory attention handles information about individual objects, while a new relational attention mechanism handles information about their relationships. The architecture therefore gives both kinds of information explicit computational roles and integrates them within the Transformer framework.

The authors evaluate DAT on synthetic relational reasoning benchmarks as well as language modeling and visual processing tasks. Their experiments show significant gains in data efficiency and parameter efficiency. These findings support adding a dedicated relational mechanism as a way to improve learning across the tested settings. The contribution is an architectural change that makes relationship processing explicit, with empirical evidence that this structure helps models use data and parameters more effectively.
icml-2025-disentangling-and-integrating-.tldr: Dual Attention Transformers explicitly process object properties and relationships through separate attention mechanisms, improving data and parameter efficiency in experiments.

paragraphs: Adversarial training affects model families differently: improvements in robustness do not always come with the same changes in generalization. This paper explains those patterns through the manifold conjecture, which views data as occupying a lower-dimensional structure. In its explanation, adversarial examples outside that structure improve robustness, while examples on it improve generalization.

The authors connect this distinction to intrinsic dimensionality across network layers. They find low intrinsic dimensionality earlier in vision and decoder-based models, favoring off-manifold examples, and later in encoder-based models, favoring on-manifold examples. This links where perturbations are applied to the kind of training benefit they can produce.

Using that observation, the authors introduce SMAAT for encoder-based models. It perturbs the layer with the lowest intrinsic dimensionality, shortening the projected gradient descent process used to generate adversarial examples. The reported GPU-time reduction is 25–33%, alongside significantly improved robustness. Evaluations spanning text generation, sentiment classification, safety filtering, and retrieval-augmented generation show stronger robustness with generalization comparable to standard training.
icml-2025-explaining-the-role-of-intrins.tldr: SMAAT uses layerwise intrinsic dimensionality to target adversarial perturbations, improving robustness while reducing GPU time in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Training losses summarize performance on observed examples, but their relationship to performance on unseen data needs justification. This paper studies tilted empirical risk, a nonlinear loss summary based on exponential tilting. It focuses on negative tilt, the regime associated with robustness, and analyzes the difference between population risk and the tilted training risk.

The authors provide uniform and information-theoretic bounds even when individual losses are unbounded. Their assumption is that the loss has a bounded moment of order 1+ε, with ε between zero and one. Under these conditions, the stated convergence rate is O(n^(−ε/(1+ε))), where n counts training samples. This establishes an application of negative-tilt risk even without distribution shift.

The paper separately studies noisy training outliers and gives robustness guarantees under distribution shift. Simple experiments support the analysis and use the bounds to choose the tilt from data. The work therefore connects a robustness-oriented training criterion to both generalization guarantees and a principled way to set its controlling parameter.
icml-2025-generalization-and-robustness-.tldr: The paper establishes conditional generalization and robustness guarantees for negative-tilt empirical risk and uses the bounds to guide tilt selection.

paragraphs: Similarity search can return many points that are close to a query but largely duplicate one another. A common solution retrieves a large candidate pool and then selects a smaller, more diverse subset. This paper targets the resulting inefficiency: finding a small final answer may require retrieving far more candidates first.

The authors develop graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor algorithms that incorporate diversity constraints directly into search. Their design builds on popular graph-search methods, allowing it to use existing efficient implementations. The approach combines the goals of closeness and diversity within the retrieval procedure, bypassing the usual retrieve-then-filter process.

For datasets with low intrinsic dimension, the authors prove a search-time bound depending only on the requested result count k and log Δ, where Δ compares the dataset's diameter with its closest-pair distance. They describe this as qualitatively similar to bounds for standard graph search without diversity constraints. Experiments also show substantially lower search time than the two-stage approach, supporting the practical value of enforcing diversity during retrieval.
icml-2025-graph-based-algorithms-for-div.tldr: Graph-based search algorithms retrieve diverse approximate neighbors directly, reducing search time and providing efficiency guarantees for low-intrinsic-dimensional data.

paragraphs: Link prediction evaluates whether a model can distinguish hidden graph edges from node pairs that are not connected. This paper questions a common way of constructing that evaluation. The authors show that the usual edge-sampling procedure implicitly favors high-degree nodes, meaning nodes with many connections receive a systematically different role in the benchmark.

That bias can reward methods that rely heavily on degree instead of learning richer graph structure. In the studied setting, a null method using node degree alone can achieve nearly optimal performance. The result matters because a strong benchmark score may partly reflect the sampling procedure rather than the structural understanding the benchmark is intended to measure.

The authors propose a degree-corrected benchmark that gives a more reasonable assessment and better matches performance on recommendation tasks. They also demonstrate benefits when using the corrected setup to train graph models. Reducing the incentive to overfit node degrees helps the models learn relevant graph structures, so the correction affects both evaluation quality and what training encourages.
icml-2025-implicit-degree-bias-in-the-li.tldr: Common link-prediction sampling can reward degree-based shortcuts, while a degree-corrected benchmark improves assessment and encourages learning relevant graph structure.

paragraphs: Pipeline parallelism divides a neural network into stages across interconnected devices, allowing large models to be trained on smaller machines. Asynchronous optimization keeps the pipeline fully utilized by construction. Its difficulty is that computation and updates no longer stay synchronized: a gradient may describe an older version of the weights than the one being updated.

The authors adapt Nesterov Accelerated Gradient to address this delay. Their main change is to its look-ahead step, modifying how the optimizer anticipates an update so that it can better accommodate stale gradients. They prove a sublinear convergence rate when the gradient delay is fixed, giving a theoretical guarantee for that specified delay setting.

Experiments use decoder-only language models with as many as one billion parameters. In these tests, the proposed optimizer significantly outperforms existing asynchronous methods and even exceeds the synchronous baseline. The findings suggest that changing the optimizer to account for delayed gradients can make high pipeline utilization compatible with strong training performance in the evaluated language-modeling workloads.
icml-2025-nesterov-method-for-asynchrono.tldr: A modified Nesterov look-ahead step handles stale pipeline gradients, with fixed-delay convergence guarantees and strong language-modeling results.

paragraphs: NETS addresses sampling from distributions whose probabilities are known only up to a normalizing factor. It starts with an easy base distribution and transports samples toward the target over a finite time. This follows non-equilibrium sampling approaches, where evolving importance weights correct for discrepancies that remain during the transport.

In the continuous-time formulation, sample paths follow Langevin dynamics under a changing potential, while corrective weights evolve according to Jarzynski's equality. NETS adds a learned drift that reduces the variance of those weights. Its objective can be estimated without backpropagation and provably bounds the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the estimated distribution and the target, linking the learning criterion to distributional accuracy.

The method provides unbiased samples and includes a diffusion coefficient that can be adjusted after training to improve effective sample size. This separates some sampling adjustments from learning the drift. Experiments cover standard benchmarks, high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures, and statistical lattice field theory models, where the authors report compelling performance across these different sampling settings.
icml-2025-nets-a-non-equilibrium-transpo.tldr: NETS learns a transport drift that reduces corrective-weight variance when sampling unnormalized distributions, with a provable distributional bound.

paragraphs: Shapley values assign contributions to features when explaining a model's prediction, with desirable theoretical properties for that attribution. Usually, these explanations are calculated after a prediction has been made, adding computation at inference time. This paper proposes ViaSHAP, which makes learned Shapley-value computation part of the predictive model itself.

ViaSHAP learns a function that produces the feature contributions, then obtains predictions by summing them. Prediction and explanation therefore come from the same learned computation. The authors explore two implementations: one motivated by the universal approximation theorem and another by the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem. These provide different routes to constructing the function that predicts contributions.

A large empirical study finds that the implementation using Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks matches state-of-the-art algorithms on tabular prediction tasks. Its explanations are also significantly more accurate than those of FastSHAP on tabular data and images. The results show that directly learning attributions can support competitive prediction quality while improving explanation accuracy against the tested approximation method.
icml-2025-prediction-via-shapley-value-r.tldr: ViaSHAP learns feature attributions whose sum gives predictions, achieving competitive tabular performance and more accurate explanations than FastSHAP.

paragraphs: Learning representations for three-dimensional medical scans is challenging because volumetric models are computationally expensive and large training collections are difficult to assemble. Raptor addresses this by generating volume embeddings without additional training. It reuses a frozen two-dimensional foundation model that was pretrained on natural images.

The method processes individual cross-sections of a medical volume to extract visual tokens. It then compresses these tokens spatially using random projections. This combination lets it draw on an existing image representation while reducing the computation needed to represent a full volume. The aim is to preserve useful semantic information through a compact representation of the cross-sectional features.

Across ten medical-volume tasks, the authors report better performance than state-of-the-art methods, including models pretrained specifically on medical volumes. The abstract lists improvements ranging from 3% to 14% against the named alternatives. These findings support the usefulness of frozen natural-image features combined with random spatial compression for volumetric tasks, while avoiding the costly training otherwise needed to produce the proposed embeddings.
icml-2025-raptor-scalable-train-free-emb.tldr: Raptor creates medical-volume embeddings without additional training by combining frozen 2D image features with random spatial projections.

paragraphs: Graph transformers need structural information alongside attention to distinguish different graph patterns. Relative Random Walk Probabilities, or RRWP, provide such information through edge representations. However, the authors identify cases where RRWP cannot distinguish edges belonging to different local structures, limiting how much graph detail those representations communicate.

The proposed Simple Path Structural Encoding, or SPSE, instead encodes edges using counts of simple paths, which do not revisit nodes. The authors show theoretically and experimentally that this captures structural distinctions missed by RRWP, particularly local cyclic patterns. Because counting simple paths can be computationally demanding, they also develop an efficient approximation algorithm to make the encoding practical.

SPSE improves performance over RRWP on several benchmarks, including molecular graphs and datasets requiring long-range graph reasoning. The paper reports statistically significant gains in discriminative tasks. These results indicate that changing the structural information supplied to a graph transformer can improve its predictive ability: a richer edge encoding helps expose patterns that the previous representation could leave indistinguishable.
icml-2025-simple-path-structural-encodin.tldr: SPSE uses approximate simple-path counts to give graph transformers richer structural information and improve performance over random-walk edge encodings.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct an underlying image from measurements. Diffusion models can support this by modifying their reverse sampling process to account for the observed data. Existing modifications can struggle with measurement noise, nonlinear tasks, and errors introduced earlier in sampling, often requiring many sampling or optimization steps.

The authors formulate three consistency conditions and build SITCOM around them. The method combines measurement consistency on the data manifold and forward-diffusion consistency with a new backward-diffusion condition enforced step by step and regularized by the network. At every sampling step, it optimizes the input to the pretrained model, helping maintain a consistent diffusion trajectory as reconstruction proceeds.

Enforcing these conditions, either implicitly or explicitly, allows SITCOM to use significantly fewer reverse steps. Experiments span linear and nonlinear reconstruction tasks with natural and medical images. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, the method achieves competitive or better image-similarity measurements and runtime. The results connect maintaining consistency throughout the trajectory with more efficient reconstruction in the tested settings.
icml-2025-sitcom-step-wise-triple-consis.tldr: SITCOM enforces three forms of consistency during diffusion reconstruction, reducing reverse steps while achieving competitive or better quality and runtime.

paragraphs: Bias-mitigation methods often operate on defined groups of examples, but the choice of groups can receive less attention than the method itself. This paper investigates whether subgroup definition helps explain why mitigation techniques sometimes fail. The authors systematically vary coarse, fine-grained, intersectional, and noisy groupings across vision and language classification tasks.

Their evaluation finds that subgroup choice substantially changes mitigation performance. Some definitions produce worse outcomes than applying no mitigation. This means that observing a disparity across a particular grouping is not, by itself, sufficient justification for using that same grouping to guide training. How a disparity is measured and how mitigation is organized can require different choices.

The authors provide theoretical analysis explaining these effects. In some cases, fairness for one set of subgroups improves most when mitigation uses another set. This makes subgroup definition a substantive part of the intervention, alongside the choice of algorithm. The findings support treating group construction as a way to improve both the robustness and fairness of mitigation.
icml-2025-subgroups-matter-for-robust-bi.tldr: Subgroup definitions can determine whether bias mitigation helps or harms, and the best mitigation groups may differ from the groups used to measure fairness.

paragraphs: Neural-network training depends on initialization and the randomness of stochastic gradient descent. This paper asks how far those sensitivities extend: whether tiny changes simply alter numerical weights or lead training toward meaningfully different networks. The authors find an early chaotic phase in which extremely small perturbations reliably separate otherwise identical training trajectories.

They measure separation in several complementary ways. These include distances between parameter vectors, loss barriers along interpolations between networks, and the same comparisons after aligning permutations of parameters. They also examine similarity between intermediate activations. Together, these measurements investigate differences in both the weights and the internal representations learned by the models.

The sensitivity falls rapidly as training progresses. Across different hyperparameter and fine-tuning settings, the analysis shows how perturbations can steer trajectories toward distinct loss minima. This timing matters for understanding training stability: a perturbation's effect depends on when it occurs. The findings have implications for fine-tuning, combining model weights, and understanding the diversity available in model ensembles.
icml-2025-the-butterfly-effect-neural-ne.tldr: Tiny perturbations can drive early neural-network training toward different minima, with sensitivity declining rapidly later in training.

paragraphs: Language models can struggle with structurally unfamiliar tasks even when a prompt contains a few worked examples. This paper investigates test-time training as a way to adapt to those examples. The method temporarily updates model parameters during inference using a loss derived from the input data, allowing the supplied examples to influence the model through training.

On the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, this approach achieves up to six times the accuracy of fine-tuned baselines. An eight-billion-parameter language model reaches 53.0% on the public validation set. Combining it with program-synthesis methods raises accuracy to 61.9%, a result the authors report as matching average human performance on that evaluation.

The authors also test BIG-Bench Hard. With ten examples, test-time training improves accuracy from 50.5% under standard few-shot prompting to 57.8%, a gain of 7.3 percentage points. These results show that temporary parameter adaptation can extract benefits from examples beyond what prompting alone achieves in the tested settings, supporting its potential for learning unfamiliar task structures.
icml-2025-the-surprising-effectiveness-o.tldr: Temporarily training on input examples improves language-model performance on unfamiliar reasoning tasks beyond the tested prompting and fine-tuned baselines.

paragraphs: Federated learning needs to protect participants' data while resisting malicious contributions. Achieving both with strong model utility commonly assumes a trusted central server. This paper shows that a weaker trust arrangement can suffice: every pair of participants shares a random seed that remains unknown to everyone else.

The proposed algorithm, CafCor, combines robust gradient aggregation with correlated noise generated using those shared seeds. Robust aggregation addresses malicious updates, while the noise mechanism supports privacy. The analysis allows malicious participants to cooperate with an untrusted server, so server trust is not part of the assumed protection.

The authors prove privacy–utility trade-offs that substantially improve on local differential privacy methods, which make no trust assumption, while approaching the utility of central differential privacy with a fully trusted server. Experiments on standard benchmarks support the method's practicality. The result identifies pairwise secret randomness as a useful middle ground: it supplies enough additional structure to combine privacy and robustness with strong utility in the studied setting.
icml-2025-towards-trustworthy-federated-.tldr: CafCor uses pairwise secret randomness to combine privacy and malicious-participant robustness without trusting the federated-learning server.

paragraphs: Predicting how genetic variants affect traits or disease can use annotations such as DNA accessibility and nearby bound proteins. However, neighboring variants are correlated, creating expensive matrix calculations during training. This computational bottleneck has restricted earlier approaches to smaller models and simplified summary statistics instead of fitting the full statistical likelihood.

The authors introduce DeepWAS, which uses fast linear algebra to train larger, more flexible neural networks by optimizing likelihood. The approach addresses the computation that previously constrained model fitting. This allows the study to examine whether increased model capacity and additional genomic features improve predictions when the fuller statistical objective becomes tractable.

The results reveal that model size and training objective interact. Larger models improve performance under the proposed full-likelihood approach, but offer no benefit over small models when trained on traditional summary statistics. Larger models using more features make better predictions in the reported study. The authors identify improved disease prediction and therapeutic target identification as potential applications of these advances.
icml-2025-training-flexible-models-of-ge.tldr: DeepWAS makes full-likelihood training practical for flexible genetic-effect models, revealing gains from larger models that summary-statistic training did not deliver.

paragraphs: Vision graph neural networks represent images through nodes and connections, offering a way to capture irregular semantic patterns. Adapting these models efficiently calls for methods that use their graph structure. The authors argue that existing visual prompting approaches, largely developed for Transformers, overlook useful relationships among graph nodes and edges.

Their proposed Vision Graph Prompting framework builds on the observation that semantically connected graph components exhibit low-rank properties. In plain terms, their semantic features contain structure that can be expressed through a more compact decomposition. The method combines those decomposed features with prompts on the vision graph, aiming to capture both broad structural patterns and detailed semantic dependencies.

Experiments across diverse downstream tasks show significant improvements in transfer performance for vision graph models. The method achieves results comparable to full fine-tuning while retaining parameter efficiency. This suggests that adapting prompts to the structure of the underlying representation can preserve useful graph relationships and provide an efficient way to transfer a pretrained vision graph model to new tasks.
icml-2025-vision-graph-prompting-via-sem.tldr: Vision Graph Prompting uses low-rank semantic structure to adapt vision graph models efficiently, reaching performance comparable to full fine-tuning in experiments.

paragraphs: Averaging model weights from checkpoints along a training run is a simple technique with potential benefits for training speed and generalization. This paper evaluates those benefits systematically using AlgoPerf, a large-scale optimization benchmark. The authors ask whether averaging reduces training time, improves performance on unseen data, and can replace learning-rate decay.

Across seven architectures and datasets, averaging substantially accelerates training and produces efficiency gains on every workload considered. The gains come with small implementation and memory costs. Generalization also improves, though the reported improvement is mild. This distinction makes the main empirical benefit clear: the strongest finding concerns training efficiency.

The authors then examine how averaging interacts with learning-rate annealing, which reduces the learning rate during training. Combining the two achieves the best performance in their evaluation. The findings therefore support weight averaging as a useful companion to learning-rate scheduling across the tested workloads, while giving a broader benchmark-based account of where its practical benefits arise.
icml-2025-when-where-and-why-to-average-.tldr: Checkpoint weight averaging accelerates all evaluated workloads with modest overhead, and combining it with learning-rate annealing gives the best tested performance.
